newsitem.title: THAILAND: More pain seen ahead for Thai financial system.
newsitem.headline: More pain seen ahead for Thai financial system.

text.p: More pain lies ahead for the Thai financial system on top of the hammer blow closure of 42 finance and securities firms this week, analysts said on Wednesday.

Though this radical surgery should lay the foundations for a stronger sector in future, the short-term implications were more dislocation in a financial system struggling to cope with the country's economic crisis, they said.
"I don't think we can assume this is the end. There now may be some which just voluntarily give up the unequal struggle," said Richard Henderson, head of research at Krungthai Thanakit.

After talks between Thai authorities and the International Monetary Fund the Bank of Thailand decided to stop pumping funds into the sector and suspended the firms. It closed a further 16 finance companies in June.
The bank said it spent almost 500 billion baht ($16.13 billion baht) supporting ailing firms whose deposit base and other funding sources had dried up as confidence waned.
"In the absence of bailouts life is going to be very tough for the lower tiers of the finance world whether they are banks or finance companies," Henderson said.

A restoration of confidence was still some way off since even the better operational finance firms were struggling to maintain loan portfolio quality as they awaited details of a likely painful economic package, analysts said.
The fluid situation was making it tough to reassure panicky depositors who were moving their savings towards perceived safer repositories at the larger commercial banks, analysts said.

"I think for the confidence-building process to happen it could take another six months to a year, I think also confidence remains quite poor at the medium to small sized banks," said Suraphol Thipvilai, finance and securities analyst at Vickers Ballas.
Sentiment was further threatened by depositors' perceptions that the government would be stretched to protect creditors and depositors at suspended firms, analysts said.
Total deposits at finance companies at the end of May were 912 billion baht, of which about two thirds was estimated to be in the 58 companies now suspended, analysts said.
"I think the government had to come out yesterday and say they will protect foreign creditors but in the end I think they may have some constraints doing so," Suraphol said.

Though some of the suspended firms were likely to re-emerge after a 90-day period in a revamped form, life for any of the surviving firms was likely to be tough for the next few months, analysts said.
The absence of a support package for the property sector, to which finance firms had loaned around 800 billion baht, was an immediate worry, analysts said.

This all offered little bright news in the short term for the 26 operational listed finance and securities firms whose shareholders should expect a round of rights issues to help recapitalise even the best managed firms, analysts said.
